The '''2026 Arizona gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Arizona]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Katie Hobbs]] is seeking a second term. She is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[United States House of Representatives|congressman]] [[Andy Biggs]].

[[Primary elections]] took place on July 21, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}}</ref> Hobbs secured the Democratic nomination unopposed. Biggs secured the Republican nomination over congressman [[David Schweikert]] with 73.6% of the vote.<ref name=results>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/arizona-governor-results|title=Arizona Governor Primary Results|work=[[NBC News]]|access-date=July 22, 2026}}</ref>  

Following the passage of Proposition 131 in the [[2022 Arizona elections|2022 elections]], this will be the first gubernatorial election in Arizona in which candidates will be required to nominate a [[running mate]] for the newly established position of [[Lieutenant Governor of Arizona|lieutenant governor]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Arizona will elect its first lieutenant governor in 2026. What to know about the role |first=Stacey |last=Barchenger |work=[[The Arizona Republic]] |date=September 21, 2023 |access-date=October 14, 2024 |url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/arizona/2023/09/21/arizona-will-elect-its-first-lieutenant-governor-in-2026-what-to-know/70848159007/}}</ref> This will be one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]].
{{toclimit|3}}

== Background ==
Arizona is considered to be a [[purple state]] at both the federal and statewide level. After [[Joe Biden]] carried the state narrowly in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Arizona|2020 presidential election]],<ref>[https://www.cnn.com/2020/11/12/politics/biden-wins-arizona Biden carries Arizona, flipping a longtime Republican stronghold], CNN, November 13, 2020</ref> [[Donald Trump]] carried the state of Arizona by 5.5 points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Arizona|2024 presidential election]].<ref>[https://news.sky.com/story/us-election-how-big-a-win-was-this-for-donald-trump-13250701 US election: How big a win was this for Donald Trump?], Sky News, January 20, 2025</ref> Democrats control both [[U.S. Senate]] seats in Arizona<ref>[https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/11/12/democrat-gallego-wins-arizona-senate-race-defining-republican-majority Democrat Gallego wins Arizona, Republicans hold 53-47 US Senate majority], Al Jazeera, November 12, 2024</ref><ref>[https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/mark-kelly-wins-senate-race-in-arizona Mark Kelly wins Senate race in Arizona], PBS, November 12, 2022</ref> and hold the governorship, secretary of state office, and attorney general office.<ref>[https://apnews.com/article/2022-midterm-elections-arizona-governor-hobbs-ceadb2bf55f1d5ec4760f423f1af0204 Hobbs wins Arizona governor's race, flipping state for Dems], AP News, November 14, 2022</ref><ref>[https://www.multistate.us/insider/2024/11/6/post-election-republicans-add-to-strong-hold-of-state-governments Post-Election: Republicans Add to Strong Hold of State Governments], MultiState.US, November 6, 2024</ref> Meanwhile, Republicans maintain a majority in the [[Arizona Senate]] and [[Arizona House of Representatives]],<ref>[https://coppercourier.com/2024/11/20/arizona-legislature-republican-2025/ Republicans maintain total control of the Arizona Legislature. Here's what you need to know.], The Copper Courier, November 20, 2024</ref> and control 6 of the 9 [[U.S. House of Representatives|House of Representatives seats]] in the state.<ref>[https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/05/arizona-congressional-races-election-results/75904496007/ Republicans keep 6-3 majority in Arizona's US House delegation], AZ Central, November 13, 2024</ref> Democrats have characterized this race as key to establishing a Democratic [[Government trifecta|trifecta]] in Arizona for the first time in 60 years.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Romo |first=Renee |date=2025-12-12 |title=Democrats hoping for Arizona legislature trifecta |url=https://www.kold.com/2025/12/12/democrats-hoping-arizona-legislature-trifecta/ |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=[[KOLD-TV|KOLD]] |language=en}}</ref>

==Green primary==
===Background===
The [[Green Party of Arizona]] disavowed candidate Risa Lombardo, accusing her of being a Republican running to draw votes from Katie Hobbs. Lombardo, a former precinct committee member for the [[Arizona Republican Party]] and wife of a Republican activist, denied the accusations. Her campaign received services from firms and attorneys with connections to Republicans. The party supported a write-in candidate in the July 21st primary, but Lombardo obtained the nomination.<ref name="Lombardo1">{{cite news |last1=Sievers |first1=Caitlin |title=‘Sham’ Green Party candidates tied to GOP machine as they funnel cash to a mystery company |url=https://azmirror.com/2026/07/27/sham-green-party-candidates-tied-to-gop-machine-as-they-funnel-cash-to-a-mystery-company/ |access-date=September 4, 2026 |work=[[Arizona Mirror]] |date=July 27, 2026}}</ref>

In early September, it was reported that the Arizona Attorney General’s Office was investigating allegations that Lombardo's campaign, among others, had used fraudulent donations with falsified voter information to obtain public funding.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sievers |first1=Caitlin |title=Three candidates now face a criminal probe over public campaign funding fraud allegations |url=https://azmirror.com/2026/09/01/three-candidates-now-face-a-criminal-probe-over-public-campaign-funding-fraud-allegations/ |access-date=September 4, 2026 |work=[[Arizona Mirror]] |date=September 1, 2026}}</ref>

{{pp|small=yes}} {{Short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Colorado gubernatorial election | country = Colorado | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2022 Colorado gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Colorado gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | image1 = AG Phil Weiser.jpg | nominee1 = [[Phil Weiser]] | running_mate1 = Lesley Dahlkemper | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | image2 = Victor Marx (52125665777) (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Victor Marx]] | running_mate2 = George Markert | map_image = | map_caption = | title = [[Governor of Colorado|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jared Polis]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsCO}} The '''2026 Colorado gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Colorado]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Jared Polis]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. [[Primary elections]] took place on June 30, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} In the Democratic primary, Colorado Attorney General [[Phil Weiser]] defeated U.S. senator [[Michael Bennet]]. If elected, Weiser would be the second consecutive Jewish governor after Polis. The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] has not won a gubernatorial election in Colorado since [[2002 Colorado gubernatorial election|2002]] nor a statewide office since 2016.{{Cite news |last=Times |first=The New York |date=2017-08-01 |title=Colorado University Regents-At-Large Results: Heidi Ganahl Leads |url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/2016/results/colorado-university-regents-at-large |access-date=2026-04-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Republican nominee [[Victor Marx]]'s candidacy has been mired in controversy; Marx has made a number of dubious claims and has notably stated he is unsure how many people he has killed.{{Cite web |date=May 27, 2026 |title=Full interview: Colorado Republican gubernatorial candidate Victor Marx |url=https://www.9news.com/video/news/politics/full-interview-colorado-republican-gubernatorial-candidate-victor-marx/73-c7e83d54-e098-41c0-b4fb-15457b261b06 |website=9News |language=en-US |access-date=May 29, 2026}} Leading to the Republican primary, both of Marx's opponents indicated they would refuse to endorse him if he won the nomination.{{Cite web |last=Luning |first=Ernest |date=May 27, 2026 |title=Republicans Kirkmeyer, Bottoms say they won’t back Marx if he wins Colorado’s gubernatorial primary |url=https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/05/27/republicans-kirkmeyer-bottoms-say-they-wont-back-marx-if-he-wins-colorados-gubernatorial-primary/ |website=Colorado Politics |language=en-US |access-date=July 21, 2026}} == Democratic primary == === Candidates === To move forward to the primary, candidates had to petition onto the ballot or achieve 30% or more at the [[Colorado Democratic Party]] State Assembly. Michael Bennet was the only candidate to petition onto the primary ballot. All other candidates went through the State Assembly process. [[Phil Weiser]] was the only candidate to achieve 30% or more.{{cite news |work=[[Colorado Democratic Party]] |access-date=March 28, 2026 |url=https://www.coloradodems.org/press/colorado-democratic-party-concludes-2026-state-assembly-announces-results?fbclid=IwY2xjawQ1WJ9leHRuA2FlbQIxMQBicmlkETFGQmVobEtQV1Vubk5hT1M0c3J0YwZhcHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5MgABHq17U9MKJ8KzaqEtc_RpLGbfqCD74CWiN0D8uLv96FJS6y-4SGjmCPvQ-I4j_aem_tWJWw7WdgcoqyIBfcyphrw |title=Colorado Democratic Party Concludes 2026 State Assembly, Announces Results}} Bennet's petition was deemed sufficient on March 24, 2026.{{cite news |work=Colorado Secretary of State |access-date=April 15, 2026 |url=https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/elections/vote/primaryPetitionCandidates.html |title=2026 Primary Election Petition Candidates Who Submitted Petition Signatures}} ==== Nominee ==== *[[Phil Weiser]], [[Colorado Attorney General|attorney general of Colorado]] (2019–present){{cite news |last1=Paul |first1=Jesse |title=Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser launches 2026 campaign for governor |url=https://coloradosun.com/2025/01/02/phil-weiser-colorado-governor-2026/ |access-date=January 2, 2025 |work=[[The Colorado Sun]] |date=January 2, 2025}} **Running mate: Lesley Dahlkemper, [[Jefferson County, Colorado#Government and infrastructure|Jefferson County commissioner]]{{cite web|last=Paul|first=Jesse|title=Phil Weiser taps Jefferson County commissioner as running mate in Colorado governor's race|website=The Colorado Sun|date=July 22, 2026|url=https://coloradosun.com/2026/07/22/lesley-dahlhemper-phil-weiser-running-mate/|access-date=July 24, 2026}} ====Eliminated in primary==== *[[Michael Bennet]], [[U.S. senator]] (2009–present){{cite web |last1=Kim |first1=Caitlyn |title=Sen. Primary elections took place on August 11, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Ned Lamont]] is running for a third term, winning the Democratic nomination in August 2026.{{Cite news |last=Vigdor |first=Neil |date=2026-08-12 |title=Ned Lamont Wins the Democratic Primary for Connecticut Governor |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/11/us/politics/connecticut-primary-governor-lamont-elliott.html |access-date=2026-08-12 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Lamont is one of the most popular governors in the United States, with a 63% approval rating as of October 2025, according to [[Morning Consult]];{{Cite web |title=U.S. Governor Approval Rating Tracker |url=https://pro.morningconsult.com/trackers/governor-approval-ratings |access-date=2025-11-15 |website=Morning Consult Pro |language=en}} however, a [[University of New Hampshire]] poll from May 2025 found that 44% of Connecticut voters believe he should not run for a third term.{{Cite web |last=Craven |first=John |date=June 5, 2025 |title=Gov. Lamont 'seriously' considering running for a rare third term |url=https://connecticut.news12.com/gov-lamont-seriously-considering-running-for-a-rare-third-term |website=News 12 Connecticut}} [[Connecticut House of Representatives|State representative]] [[Josh Elliott (politician)|Josh Elliott]] challenged Lamont in the primary as a [[Progressivism in the United States|progressive]].{{Cite news |last=Putterman |first=Alex |title=State Rep. Josh Elliott announces campaign for governor, promising to tax CT's wealthy |url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-josh-elliott-governor-lamont-primary-challenge-20768829.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260206022833/https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-josh-elliott-governor-lamont-primary-challenge-20768829.php |archive-date=2026-02-06 |url-status=live |access-date=2026-02-06 |work=CT Insider |language=en}} {{toclimit|4}} ==Democratic primary== While incumbent [[List of governors of Connecticut|governor]] [[Ned Lamont]] initially had expressed doubts about running for a third term,{{Cite news |last=Haar |first=Dan |title=Dan Haar: Will he run? Lamont interview reveals doubts about a third term for Connecticut governor |url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-gov-ned-lamont-third-term-20243961.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250701001417/https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-gov-ned-lamont-third-term-20243961.php |archive-date=2025-07-01 |url-status=live |access-date=2025-11-15 |work=CT Insider |language=en}} he announced that he would run for re-election in November 2025.{{Cite web |last=Pazniokas |first=Mark |date=2025-11-14 |title=Today, the curtain goes up on Ned Lamont's bid for a third term |url=https://ctmirror.org/2025/11/14/gov-lamont-reelection-third-term-announcement/ |access-date=2025-11-15 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}} [[Connecticut House of Representatives|State representative]] [[Josh Elliott (politician)|Josh Elliott]] had already launched a bid to primary Lamont, believing that Connecticut needed a more [[Progressivism in the United States|progressive]] leader.{{Cite news |last=Craven |first=John |date=2025-07-14 |title=Democrat Josh Elliott launches bid for governor, promising big shift from Lamont |url=https://connecticut.news12.com/2025/07/14/democrat-josh-elliott-launches-bid-for-governor-promising-big-shift-from/4fXhwKnBB4lof6pdqcoKJs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518211332/https://connecticut.news12.com/2025/07/14/democrat-josh-elliott-launches-bid-for-governor-promising-big-shift-from/4fXhwKnBB4lof6pdqcoKJs |archive-date=2026-05-18 |access-date=2026-05-18 |work=News 12 Connecticut}} At the Democratic State Convention on May 16, 2026, at [[The Bushnell Center for the Performing Arts|The Bushnell]] in [[Hartford, Connecticut|Hartford]], Lamont defeated Elliott for the [[Democratic Party of Connecticut|state party]] endorsement, 1,468 votes (74.6%) to 501 (25.4%). However, Elliott surpassed the 15% of delegates needed to get on the ballot for the primary, which took place on August 11;{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Andrew |date=2026-05-16 |title=CT Dems endorse Lamont for 3rd term, but he faces primary |url=https://ctmirror.org/2026/05/16/lamont-clinches-ct-democratic-party-endorsement-but-will-face-primary/ |access-date=2026-05-18 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}} Lamont was the first incumbent governor to face a primary since [[Ella Grasso]] in [[1978 Connecticut gubernatorial election|1978]]. {{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2025}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Illinois gubernatorial election | country = Illinois | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2022 Illinois gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Illinois gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = JB Pritzker 2026 (cropped 3x4).jpg | nominee1 = [[JB Pritzker]] | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = [[Christian Mitchell]] | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = Darren Bailey at a 2022 Campaign Event (cropped2).jpg | nominee2 = [[Darren Bailey]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = Aaron Del Mar | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | map_image = | map_caption = | title = [[Governor of Illinois|governor]] | before_election = [[JB Pritzker]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsIL}} The '''2026 Illinois gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Illinois]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[JB Pritzker]] is seeking a third term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former nominee [[Darren Bailey]]. [[Primary elections]] were held on March 17, 2026.{{Cite web |last=Illinois State Board of Elections |title=Schedule of Future Elections |url=https://www.elections.il.gov/agencyforms/1%20SCHEDULE%20OF%20FUTURE%20ELECTIONS/Schedule%20of%20Elections%20-%20Revised.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260221135507/https://www.elections.il.gov/agencyforms/1%20SCHEDULE%20OF%20FUTURE%20ELECTIONS/Schedule%20of%20Elections%20-%20Revised.pdf |archive-date=February 21, 2026 |access-date=2025-07-21 |website=www.elections.il.gov}} Pritzker secured the Democratic nomination unopposed, while [[Darren Bailey]] secured the Republican nomination with 54% of the vote.{{cite web |title=Illinois Governor Primary Results 2026 |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/illinois-governor-results |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260411230100/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/illinois-governor-results |archive-date=April 11, 2026 |access-date=April 19, 2026 |website=[[NBC News]]}} Pritzker selected [[Christian Mitchell]] as his running mate, as incumbent lieutenant governor [[Julianna Stratton]] is the Democratic nominee for [[2026 United States Senate election in Illinois|U.S. Senate]]. This is the first gubernatorial rematch in Illinois since [[1986 Illinois gubernatorial election|1986]]. == Background == A moderately to strongly [[blue state]], Illinois has a reputation for being both the most populous and the most left-leaning state in the Midwest, traits vastly owed to the progressive and diverse [[Chicago metropolitan area]]. Though the state has historically favored Republicans for [[Governor of Illinois|governor]], Democrats have won all but one gubernatorial race in Illinois since [[2002 Illinois gubernatorial election|2002]], the exception being [[Bruce Rauner]]'s narrow victory in [[2014 Illinois gubernatorial election|2014]].{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2014 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2014&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250404104935/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2014&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2025-04-04 |access-date=2025-04-09 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} In addition, Democrats have won Illinois by double-digit margins in every presidential race since [[1992 United States presidential election in Illinois|1992]]; and consistently occupied all of its statewide offices since [[2018 Illinois elections|2019]]. Incumbent governor [[JB Pritzker]], a member of the Democratic Party, has comfortably won in the past two elections, having first been elected with a 15.6% lead in [[2018 Illinois gubernatorial election|2018]]{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2018 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2018&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520050528/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2018&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2024-05-20 |access-date=2025-04-09 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} and won re-election by 12.5% in [[2022 Illinois gubernatorial election|2022]].{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2022 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2022&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240419033643/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2022&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2024-04-19 |access-date=2025-04-09 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} Despite the state's strong Democratic lean, Republicans are comfortably favored in most of rural Illinois, especially in much of [[Forgottonia|West Central]] and [[Southern Illinois]]. Illinois is one of 16 states that do not have gubernatorial term limits. The '''2026 New York gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of New York]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Kathy Hochul]] is running for re-election to a second full term.<ref name="HochulRunning">{{Cite news |last=Parsnow |first=Luke |date=July 2, 2024 |title=Hochul says she's running for another term as New York governor in 2026 |url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2024/07/02/hochul-says-she-s-running-for-another-term-as-governor-in-2026 |access-date=August 20, 2024 |website=[[Spectrum News]] |language=en |archive-date=July 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708215410/https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2024/07/02/hochul-says-she-s-running-for-another-term-as-governor-in-2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Primary elections]] took place on June 23, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260423040741/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=April 23, 2026|access-date=August 5, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures|NCSL]]}}</ref> The gubernatorial candidates selected their running mates, instead of having separate primaries.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cuza|first=Bobby|date=May 8, 2025|title=State lawmakers eliminate lieutenant governor primary|url=https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2025/05/09/albany-lawmakers-eliminate-lieutenant-governor-primary?cid=share_clip|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260105102847/https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2025/05/09/albany-lawmakers-eliminate-lieutenant-governor-primary?cid=share_clip|archive-date=January 5, 2026|work=[[Spectrum News]] |url-status=live}}</ref> 

Hochul will face Nassau County Executive [[Bruce Blakeman]], the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] and [[Conservative Party of New York State|Conservative]] nominee, in the general election. After U.S. representative [[Elise Stefanik]] withdrew from the Republican primary in December 2025, Blakeman was endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]].<ref name=te>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/12/20/trump-new-york-governor-endorsement-bruce-blakeman-00702013|title=Trump endorses in New York governor race the day after Stefanik drops out|date=December 20, 2025|work=Politico|access-date=2026-10-10}}</ref> Republicans have not won a statewide election in New York since [[George Pataki]] was re-elected governor in [[2002 New York gubernatorial election|2002]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://abc7ny.com/post/new-york-rep-elise-stefanik-announce-run-governor-soon-friday/18122558/|title=Rep. Elise Stefanik to announce run for New York governor as soon as Friday|date=November 6, 2025|work=ABC7 New York|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251107000827/https://abc7ny.com/post/new-york-rep-elise-stefanik-announce-run-governor-soon-friday/18122558/|archive-date=2025-11-07|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Background==
Governor [[Kathy Hochul]] took office on August 24, 2021, upon the resignation of her predecessor, [[Andrew Cuomo]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/24/nyregion/kathy-hochul-governor-ny.html|title=Hochul Is Sworn In: 'I Want People to Believe in Their Government Again'|first=Luis|last=Ferré-Sadurní|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=August 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211224074148/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/24/nyregion/kathy-hochul-governor-ny.html|archive-date=2021-12-24|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> Hochul was elected to a full term in [[2022 New York gubernatorial election|2022]] with 53.1% of the vote in the closest New York gubernatorial election since [[1994 New York gubernatorial election|1994]].<ref name="results">{{cite web |title=2022 General Election Governor and Lt. Governor Results |url=https://elections.ny.gov/2022-general-election-governor-and-lt-governor-results |website=[[New York State Board of Elections]]|date=November 8, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.timesunion.com/state/article/Zeldin-concede-17571499.php|title=Zeldin concedes to Hochul in closest governor's race since 1994|first=Brendan J.|last=Lyons|date=November 9, 2022|website=Times Union|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261004233945/https://www.timesunion.com/state/article/Zeldin-concede-17571499.php|archive-date=2026-10-04|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Democratic primary==
Due to low approval ratings, poor Democratic performances in the [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections|2022 midterm elections]] in [[2022 New York state elections|New York]], and controversies surrounding her administration, Hochul was considered vulnerable to a primary challenge in 2026.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Reisman |first=Nick |date=September 5, 2024 |title=Hochul's headwinds become tougher with indictment of alleged foreign agent |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/09/05/linda-sun-arrest-hochul-approval-00177430?nname=new-york-playbook&nid=0000014f-1646-d88f-a1cf-5f46b74f0000&nrid=7fbb50ed-ea1a-4aff-a106-d6b8cc25c14a&nlid=630317 |work=[[Politico]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240923230245/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/09/05/linda-sun-arrest-hochul-approval-00177430|archive-date=2024-09-23|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> 

On June 2, 2025, following months of reports about a strained relationship with the governor's office, [[Antonio Delgado]] launched his campaign for the Democratic nomination.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Mays |first=Jeffery C. |date=June 2, 2025 |title=Antonio Delgado, Hochul's No. 2, Will Challenge Her in Governor's Race |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/02/nyregion/antonio-delgado-governor-hochul.html |access-date=June 2, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250602204431/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/02/nyregion/antonio-delgado-governor-hochul.html|archive-date=2025-06-02|url-status=live}}</ref> On February 4, 2026, he announced nurse, union organizer, and socialist activist [[India Walton]] as his running mate.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/capital-region/politics/2026/02/04/antonio-delgado-governor-election-running-mate|title=Delgado picks India Walton as running mate in governor's race|date=February 4, 2026|work=Spectrum Local News|access-date=2026-10-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260210185600/https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/capital-region/politics/2026/02/04/antonio-delgado-governor-election-running-mate|archive-date=2026-02-10|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Despite early perceptions of vulnerability to a left-wing challenge, Hochul was endorsed in February 2026 by [[Zohran Mamdani]] and [[Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez]], both prominent members of the [[New York City Democratic Socialists of America]]. ''[[Politico]]'' noted that the endorsements "all but crowd out her little-known primary challenger, (Antonio) Delgado," while Democratic strategist Trip Yang called Hochul "the comeback player of the year."<ref name="embrace">{{cite news |title=Why the left decided to embrace, and not fight, Kathy Hochul |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/06/why-the-left-decided-to-embrace-and-not-fight-kathy-hochul-00769785 |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=2026-02-08 |language=en |date=2026-02-06|last=Reisman|first=Nick}}</ref> She was soon endorsed by the [[New York State Democratic Party|New York Democratic Party]] after securing 85% of support from party members at the state convention.<ref>{{cite news |title=Hochul projects 'strength' as she resoundingly wins Democratic backing for a new term |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/06/hochul-projects-strength-as-she-resoundingly-wins-democratic-backing-for-a-new-term-00769561 |work=Politico |access-date=2026-02-13 |language=en |date=2026-02-06}}</ref>  Delgado ended his campaign on February 10, 2026, citing a lack of a viable path forward.<ref name=Sterne>{{Cite news |last1=Sterne |first1=Peter |last2=Lewis |first2=Rebecca |date=February 10, 2026 |title=Antonio Delgado ends his campaign for governor |url=https://www.cityandstateny.com/politics/2026/02/antonio-delgado-ends-his-campaign-governor/411320/ |access-date=2026-02-10 |work=City & State |language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260212094733/https://www.cityandstateny.com/politics/2026/02/antonio-delgado-ends-his-campaign-governor/411320/|archive-date=2026-02-12|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Republican primary==
U.S. representative [[Elise Stefanik]] was considered a potential gubernatorial candidate throughout 2025. She formally announced her candidacy on November 7, 2025.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rep. Elise Stefanik announces run for New York governor, challenging Kathy Hochul in 2026 election - CBS New York |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/elise-stefanik-running-for-new-york-governor/ |website=CBS |access-date=November 7, 2025 |date=November 7, 2025}}</ref> A July 2025 Siena poll showed Stefanik leading two other potential Republican gubernatorial candidates, U.S. representative [[Mike Lawler]] and Nassau County executive [[Bruce Blakeman]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2025/06/30/poll--stefanik-leads-potential-gop-field-for-n-y--governor|title=Poll: Stefanik leads potential GOP field for N.Y. governor; Hochul leads all 3|work=Spectrum Local News|last=Parsnow|first=Luke}}</ref> In May 2025, President [[Donald Trump]] endorsed Lawler and Blakeman for re-election to their current posts "in a not-so-subtle attempt to clear the field for upstate Congresswoman Elise Stefanik to get the GOP nomination".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/trump-bruce-blakeman-mike-lawler-endorsements/|title=Ahead of N.Y. governor's race, President Trump's endorsements send "loud message" |last=Kramer|first=Marcia|date=May 7, 2025|website=CBS News|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305092233/https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/trump-bruce-blakeman-mike-lawler-endorsements/|archive-date=2026-03-05|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> On July 23, 2025, Mike Lawler announced that he would run for re-election to Congress.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Anderson |first1=Renee |last2=Kramer |first2=Marcia |last3=Woodall |first3=Hunter |date=July 23, 2025 |title=Mike Lawler to sit out New York governor's race and run for reelection in House district |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/mike-lawler-reelection-new-york-governor-race-elise-stefanik-republicans/ |access-date=2026-10-10 |work=[[CBS News]] |language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305092233/https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/trump-bruce-blakeman-mike-lawler-endorsements/|archive-date=2026-03-05|url-status=live}}</ref>

Bruce Blakeman was re-elected to the post of Nassau County executive by a double-digit margin in November 2025.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://gothamist.com/news/blakeman-reelected-as-nassau-county-exec-and-gop-hopes-for-a-bulwark-against-mamdani|title=Blakeman reelected as Nassau County exec and GOP hopes for a bulwark against Mamdani|first=Jimmy|last=Vielkind|date=November 5, 2025|website=Gothamist|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260206133736/https://gothamist.com/news/blakeman-reelected-as-nassau-county-exec-and-gop-hopes-for-a-bulwark-against-mamdani|archive-date=2026-02-06|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> When asked about Blakeman's potential gubernatorial candidacy, Trump stated that Blakeman and Stefanik were "both great people".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://abcnews.com/Politics/county-gop-leader-bruce-blakeman-announces-run-new/story?id=128244979|title=County GOP leader Bruce Blakeman announces run for New York governor, taking on fellow Trump ally Elise Stefanik|first=Oren|last=Oppenheim|website=ABC News|date=December 9, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260206133736/https://gothamist.com/news/blakeman-reelected-as-nassau-county-exec-and-gop-hopes-for-a-bulwark-against-mamdani|archive-date=2026-02-06|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> On December 9, 2025, Blakeman launched his campaign for the 2026 Republican gubernatorial nomination.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kramer |first=Marcia |last2=Capellini |first2=Jeff |last3=Westbrook |first3=Elijah |date=2025-12-09 |title=Bruce Blakeman announces run for New York governor, to challenge Elise Stefanik in Republican primary |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/bruce-blakeman-running-for-new-york-governor-2026/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251209152008/https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/bruce-blakeman-running-for-new-york-governor-2026/ |archive-date=2025-12-09 |access-date=2026-10-10 |work=CBS News}}</ref> According to ''[[The New York Times]]'', Trump's decision to remain neutral and not to attempt to clear the field for Stefanik "sent shock waves through Republican ==Conservative convention==
The [[New York State Conservative Party]] held its annual conference and nominating convention in Albany in February 2026, officially endorsing Blakeman for governor. Because New York utilizes a fusion voting system, Blakeman accepted the third-party ballot line to run concurrently on both the Republican and Conservative lines.<ref name="ConservativeLine">{{cite news |title=Bruce Blakeman receives nomination for governor from NY State Conservative Party |url=https://longisland.news12.com/bruce-blakeman-receives-nomination-for-governor-from-ny-state-conservative-party |work=News 12 |access-date=2026-02-15}}</ref>
===Candidates===
====Nominee====
*[[Bruce Blakeman]], [[Nassau County Executive|Nassau County executive]] (2021–present)<ref name="ConservativeLine"/>
**Running mate: Todd Hood, [[Madison County, New York|Madison County]] sheriff (2018–present)<ref name="HoodLtGov"/>

==Working Families convention==
The [[Working Families Party|New York Working Families Party]] declined to nominate Hochul or Delgado, instead opting for a "placeholder candidate" to appear on their ballot line. The party has stated that the placeholder candidate will later be replaced by the Democratic nominee.<ref name="Placeholder"/> A convention attendee told ''[[City & State]]'' that Delgado won 41% of the weighted party committee vote to Hochul's 3%, while "placeholder candidate" won 56% of the vote. State party leaders Jasmine Gripper and [[Ana María Archila]] disputed the claim, but did not share the exact vote totals.<ref name="Placeholder"/>

On August 21, the Working Families Party nominated Hochul and Adams.<ref name="WFPLine"/>

The '''2026 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Pennsylvania]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Josh Shapiro]] is seeking a second term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state treasurer [[Stacy Garrity]].

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 26, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|access-date=September 27, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref> Shapiro and Garrity secured their nominations unopposed. This is one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. If elected, Garrity would be the first female governor of Pennsylvania.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Tannenbaum|first=Michael|date=August 15, 2025|title=Pa. Treasurer Stacy Garrity to run for governor against Josh Shapiro|url=https://www.phillyvoice.com/stacy-garrity-pennsylvania-governor-2026-republican-shapiro/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250818172457/https://www.phillyvoice.com/stacy-garrity-pennsylvania-governor-2026-republican-shapiro/|archive-date=August 18, 2025|access-date=May 25, 2026|work=Philly Voice}}</ref>

== Background ==
[[Pennsylvania]] is a [[purple state]] located in the [[Northeastern United States]]. A part of the [[Rust Belt]], it was narrowly won by Republican [[Donald Trump]] in [[2024 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|his non-consecutive second victory in 2024]] after similarly narrow victories by Democrat [[Joe Biden]] in [[2020 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2020]] and Trump in his first election in [[2016 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2016]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/revisit-pennsylvania-election-results/|title=Revisit Pennsylvania election results from 2020 and 2016 ahead of Election Day 2024 - CBS News|date=November 4, 2024|website=www.cbsnews.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The 2024 presidential election was close, not a landslide |url=https://abcnews.go.com/538/2024-presidential-election-close-landslide/story?id=116240898 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126224157/https://abcnews.go.com/538/2024-presidential-election-close-landslide/story?id=116240898 |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 26, 2024 |website=ABC News}}</ref>

The state has a Democratic and Republican senator, making it one of only three states to have a split Senate delegation,{{efn|The other two are [[Maine]], with an independent who caucuses with the Democrats and a Republican, and [[Wisconsin]], with a Democrat and a Republican.<ref>[https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2024/11/19/119th-congress-smashes-record-low-for-number-of-split-us-senate-delegations/ 119th Congress Smashes Record Low for Number of Split US Senate Delegations], Smart Politics, November 19, 2024. Retrieved January 31, 2026</ref>}} while Republicans hold a majority in the state's House delegation, with ten seats to the Democrats' seven.<ref>{{cite news |title=119th Congress Smashes Record Low for Number of Split US Senate Delegations |url=https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2024/11/19/119th-congress-smashes-record-low-for-number-of-split-us-senate-delegations/ |access-date=September 4, 2025 |issue=Smart Politics |date=November 19, 2024}}</ref> Democrats also control the [[Pennsylvania House of Representatives]] while Republicans control the [[Pennsylvania Senate]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Democrats will again control Pennsylvania House after holding on to one-seat majority |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/11/pennsylvania-election-results-2024-state-house-democratic-republican-control/ |access-date=September 4, 2025 |publisher=Spotlight PA |date=November 8, 2024}}</ref> 

Republicans have not won a Pennsylvania gubernatorial election since [[2010 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|2010]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Josh Shapiro]] was first elected with 56.5% of the vote in  [[2022 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|2022]], succeeding term-limited Democrat [[Tom Wolf]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://penncapital-star.com/campaigns-elections/inside-josh-shapiros-2022-landslide-and-what-it-means-for-2024-analysis/|title=Inside Josh Shapiro's 2022 landslide -- and what it means for 2024 | Analysis • Pennsylvania Capital-Star|first=Nick|last=Field|date=May 21, 2023}}</ref>

==General election==
===Campaign===
A major issue in the general election has been the growing [[opposition to AI data centers]], similarly experienced throughout the country. Shapiro, despite having previously supported the construction of two [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] data center campuses estimated at $20 million the previous year and being quoted as saying Pennsylvania was "all in on AI",<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cityandstatepa.com/policy/2026/05/gov-josh-shapiros-new-data-center-standards-reflect-new-reality/413789/|title=Gov. Josh Shapiro's new data center standards reflect new reality|first1=Justin|last1=Sweitzer|first2=Harrison|last2=Cann|website=[[City & State]]|date=May 27, 2026|access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref> signed an executive order in August 2026 that implemented new regulations on them and eliminated fast-tracking of approvals to build them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://whyy.org/articles/shapiro-data-centers-executive-order-pennsylvania/|title=Pennsylvania Gov. Shapiro signs wide-ranging executive order reining in data center development|first=Susan|last=Phillips|publisher=[[WHYY-TV]]|date=August 19, 2026|access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref> Garrity has criticized Shapiro for this, claiming he "sold us out" for his prior support of Amazon's $20 million data center projects, although Garrity has similarly made comments supportive of AI data centers in the past and to which Shapiro has also capitalized on.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6055856-shapiro-garrity-pennsylvania-data-center-ads/|title=Shapiro, Garrity accuse each other of supporting data centers|first=Mira|last=Bhakta|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=August 27, 2026|access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref>

he '''2026 United States Senate election in Idaho''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Idaho]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Jim Risch]] is seeking a fourth term. He is being challenged by [[Independent politician|independent]] former state representative [[Todd Achilles]]. 

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 19.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 26, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|url-status=live|access-date=September 27, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref> Risch won the Republican nomination with 67.3% of the vote, facing minimal opposition. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nomination was won by realtor David Roth, who was the nominee in [[2022 United States Senate election in Idaho|2022]], but after Achilles entered the race in July with the support of Democratic leaders, Roth withdrew near the end of the month.<ref name="Roth">{{cite web|url=https://idahocapitalsun.com/2026/07/28/idaho-democrat-david-roth-ends-campaign-for-us-senate-seat-held-by-risch/|title=Idaho Democrat David Roth ends campaign for US Senate seat held by Risch|last=Guido|first=Laura|date=July 28, 2026|access-date=July 28, 2026|website=[[States Newsroom|Idaho Capital Sun]]}}</ref>

Republicans have not lost a Senate race in Idaho since [[1974 United States Senate election in Idaho|1974]].<ref name="IdahoSenators">{{cite web |title=Idaho Senators |url=https://www.senate.gov/states/ID/senators.htm |website=[[United States Senate]] |access-date=October 24, 2026}}</ref><ref name="DemocraticPropsects">{{cite web |last1=Gonzales |first1=Nathan |title=Idaho Senate: Democratic Prospects Still Slim |url=https://insideelections.com/idaho-senate-democratic-prospects-still-slim/ |website=[[Inside Elections]] |access-date=October 24, 2026 |date=August 27, 2007}}</ref>

== Background ==
Idaho is considered a [[red state]].<ref>{{cite web |last = |first = |title = The Road To Red: How One Political Party Came To Dominate Idaho |website = NPR/Bosie State Public Radio |date = |url = https://www.boisestatepublicradio.org/the-road-to-red-how-one-political-party-came-to-dominate-idaho |accessdate = October 21, 2026}}</ref>

This is one of three races (along with [[2026 United States Senate election in Nebraska|Nebraska]] and [[2026 United States Senate election in South Dakota|South Dakota]]) in the [[2026 United States Senate elections|2026 Senate election cycle]] where the Democratic nominee has withdrawn from the race.<ref>{{cite news |last = Shane Goldmacher |first = Shane Goldmacher |title = Democrat Quits Senate Race in South Dakota, Clearing Way for Independent |newspaper = The New York Times |date = August 4, 2026 |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/04/us/politics/julian-beaudion-drops-out-south-dakota.html |accessdate = October 12, 2026}}</ref>

== General election ==
=== Campaign ===
On July 8, 2026, the Ada County Democratic Central Committee sent Roth a letter giving him until August 12 to prove that his campaign "has turned a corner" by raising $50,000 and producing a campaign plan, or the committee would consider endorsing independent candidate Todd Achilles instead. The committee said it was concerned that Roth's campaign was "not positioned to meet the moment” and argued that "we can't afford to let this moment slip away in the best political environment Idaho has seen in decades." Roth called the demands "completely ridiculous" and said he had no intention of complying, while accusing local Democratic leaders of trying to force him out of the race in favor of Achilles.<ref>{{cite news |last=Donovan Smith |first=Orion |title=Idaho They think Jim Risch could be beaten, but they aren't sure they want a Democrat to run for Senate |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/jul/18/idaho-democrats-think-jim-risch-could-be-beaten-bu/ |access-date=July 25, 2026 |work=[[The Spokesman-Review]] |date=July 18, 2026}}</ref> On July 28, Roth announced he would drop out of the race.<ref name="Roth"/>

{{Short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States Senate elections}} {{Distinguish|2026 Maine State Senate election}} {{Use American English|date=November 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=October 2026}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 United States Senate election in Maine | country = Maine | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2020 United States Senate election in Maine | previous_year = 2020 | next_election = 2032 United States Senate election in Maine | next_year = ''2032'' | election_date = {{Start date|2026|11|03}} | turnout = | image1 = Susan Collins During Senate Appropriation Homeland Security Subcommittee Hearing 8 May 2025.jpg | nominee1 = [[Susan Collins]] | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = Troy Jackson in the Senate Chamber (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Troy Jackson]] (replacing [[Graham Platner]]) | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | map = | map_caption = County results | title = U.S. senator | before_election = [[Susan Collins]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsME}} The '''2026 United States Senate election in Maine''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Maine]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Susan Collins]] is seeking a sixth term. She is being challenged by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former state Senate president [[Troy Jackson]]. The election will be conducted with [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]]. In the June 9 primaries, Collins was the only candidate to qualify for the Republican nomination. Sullivan harbor master [[Graham Platner]] won the Democratic primary over Governor [[Janet Mills]] with the support of progressive leaders, but withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault accusations and other controversies. Jackson was chosen to replace Platner through a [[Party conference#United States|nominating convention]] on July 25. As Collins is the only Republican senator representing a state that President [[Donald Trump]] did not win in any of his three presidential campaigns, the race is considered to be among the most competitive in 2026. Democrats have not won a Senate election in Maine since [[1988 United States Senate election in Maine|1988]].{{efn|[[Angus King]], who was elected in [[2012 United States Senate election in 2026}} filing his withdrawal two days later. == Democratic nominating convention == === Process === No political party in Maine had replaced their nominee in any prior election. While the exact process to be used was not immediately certain, Maine Democratic Party officials and others like [[Maine Senate]] president [[Mattie Daughtry]] called for an open and inclusive process.{{cite web |last1=Mundry |first1=Jackie |title=How does the state Democratic party choose a new candidate? |url=https://www.wmtw.com/article/how-does-maine-democratic-party-choose-new-candidate/71857778 |website=[[WMTW (TV)|WMTW]] |date=July 7, 2026 |access-date=July 8, 2026}} On July 8, the Maine Democratic Party voted to hold a state [[Party conference#United States|party convention]] to nominate a candidate to replace Platner as the Democratic nominee. The convention was held on July 25 in [[Bangor, Maine|Bangor]].{{cite web |title=Democrats in Maine formally nominate Troy Jackson as their new candidate for U.S. Senate|url=https://www.npr.org/2026/07/25/nx-s1-5902982/democrats-maine-senate-race|website=[[NPR]] |access-date=July 25, 2026|date=July 25, 2026|last=Moore|first=Elena}} In order to qualify for the {{ElectionsNC}}
The '''2026 United States Senate election in North Carolina''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[North Carolina]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former party chair [[Michael Whatley]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former governor [[Roy Cooper]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Thom Tillis]] is not seeking a third term.

Considered vulnerable to a primary challenge due to his moderate positions, Tillis announced he would run for re-election, but withdrew after voting against the [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]]. Whatley, who emerged as the Republican frontrunner after being endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], won the nomination with 64.6% of the vote over author [[Don Brown (author, born 1960)|Don Brown]]. Cooper won the Democratic nomination with 92% of the vote, facing minimal opposition.

Democrats have not won a Senate election in North Carolina since [[2008 United States Senate election in North Carolina|2008]].

== Background ==
A [[swing state]], North Carolina is considered to be a [[Red states and blue states|purple to slightly red]] Southern state at the federal level. It was also a top battleground state in the [[2020 United States presidential election in North Carolina|2020]] and [[2024 United States presidential election in North Carolina|2024]] presidential elections. The state backed [[Donald Trump]] in both elections by 1.3%<ref>{{Cite web|title=November 03, 2020 General Election Results by Contest|url=https://s3.amazonaws.com/dl.ncsbe.gov/State_Board_Meeting_Docs/2020-11-24/Canvass/State%20Composite%20Abstract%20Report%20-%20Contest.pdf|work=North Carolina State Board of Elections}}</ref> and 3.2%,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dl.ncsbe.gov/?prefix=State_Board_Meeting_Docs/2024-11-26/Canvass/ |title=NC - State_Composite_Abstract_Report-Contest.pdf |date=November 26, 2024|access-date=December 30, 2024}}</ref> respectively.

Both parties have seen success in the state in recent years. Republicans control both chambers of the [[North Carolina General Assembly]] and hold a majority in North Carolina's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] delegation,<ref name="2024fedelection">
State Board of Elections. ''[https://er.ncsbe.gov/?election_dt=11/05/2024&county_id=0&office=FED&contest=0 General election results for Federal offices, 2024]''. North Carolina State Board of Elections. Archived at [https://web.archive.org/web/20240724000000/https://er.ncsbe.gov/?election_dt=11/05/2024&county_id=0&office=FED&contest=0 Web Archive].
</ref> as well as both of the state's U.S. Senate seats. In [[2024 North Carolina Council of State elections|2024]], Democrats won half of the state's [[North Carolina Council of State|executive offices]], flipping a net of one seat from Republicans.<ref name=2024generalncsbe>{{Cite web|url=https://er.ncsbe.gov/?election_dt=11/05/2024&county_id=0&office=COS&contest=0|title=NC SBE Contest Results|website=er.ncsbe.gov}}</ref>

Democrats have not won a Senate election in North Carolina since [[Kay Hagan]] defeated [[Elizabeth Dole]] in [[2008 United States Senate election in North Carolina|2008]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/north-carolina-senate-primary-results-midterm-elections-2026/|title=Whatley, Cooper win North Carolina primaries, CBS News projects, teeing up key Senate contest|publisher=CBS News|website=CBS News|access-date=2026-10-14}}</ref>

==Republican primary==
Senator [[Thom Tillis]] was considered vulnerable to a primary challenger from his right. On June 10, 2023, the [[North Carolina Republican Party]] voted to censure Tillis for his support for the [[Respect for Marriage Act]] and immigration reform attempts.<ref>{{cite news |publisher=[[CNN]] |date=June 11, 2023 |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/06/11/politics/thom-tillis-north-carolina-gop-censure/index.html |author1=Berryman, Kim |author2=Pellish, Aaron |title=Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is censured by North Carolina GOP delegates at convention}}</ref><ref name="WRALTillisSpotlight">{{cite news |title=Trump nominations put NC's Thom Tillis, the nation's 'most vulnerable' Republican senator, in the spotlight |url=https://www.wral.com/story/trump-nominations-put-nc-s-thom-tillis-the-nation-s-most-vulnerable-republican-senator-in-the-spotlight/21724608/ |access-date=November 17, 2024 |publisher=[[WRAL-TV]] |author1=Specht, Paul |author2=Doran, Will |date=November 17, 2024 |language=en}}</ref> On June 28, 2025, President [[Donald Trump]] stated he was considering backing a primary challenger after Tillis voted against a motion to consider the [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 29, 2025 |title=Trump threatens Tillis with primary challenge |url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2025/06/28/congress/donald-trump-threatens-thom-tillis-00431472 |access-date=June 29, 2025 |website=[[Politico]] |author=Jacobs, Ben|language=en}}</ref> The following day, Tillis announced that he would not seek re-election.<ref name="Tillis">{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/06/29/thom-tillis-retires-00432045|title=Thom Tillis says he will retire following Trump attacks|last=Carney|first=Jordain|date=June 29, 2025|access-date=June 29, 2025|website=[[Politico]]}}</ref>

==Democratic primary==

[[File:Wiley Nickel endorsing Roy Cooper for Senate.jpg|thumb|Wiley Nickel endorsing Roy Cooper for Senate]]

In 2025, Roy Cooper announced his candidacy for the United States Senate seat in the 2026 election. Shortly after his announcement, former U.S. Representative [[Wiley Nickel]], who had previously entered the race, withdrew his candidacy and endorsed Cooper for the Democratic nomination.<ref>{{cite news |last=Robertson |first=Gary D. |title=Former Congressman Wiley Nickel drops out of 2026 Senate race, endorses Roy Cooper |url=https://abc11.com/post/former-congressman-wiley-nickel-drops-2026-senate-race-endorses-north-carolina-governor-roy-cooper/17348739/
 |work=Associated Press |date=July 29, 2025}}</ref> Nickel cited Cooper's executive experience and electoral strength as reasons for his endorsement.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wiley Nickel exits North Carolina Senate race the day after Roy Cooper announces candidacy |url=https://apnews.com/article/d9da6af3c46da5a96df6c7ba5ada3ae9
 |work=Associated Press |date=July 29, 2025}}</ref>

[[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Ben Ray Luján]] is seeking a second term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former oil and gas operator Larry Marker. [[Primary election]]s were held on June 2. Luján won the Democratic nomination with 83.7% of the vote against minimal opposition. After no Republicans qualified for the primary ballot, Marker was nominated as a write-in candidate. Republicans have not won a Senate election in New Mexico since [[2002 United States Senate election in New Mexico|2002]]. == Democratic primary == [[Ben Ray Luján]], a member of the Luján political The '''2026 United States Senate special election in Ohio''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Ohio]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] appointee [[Jon Husted]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former senator [[Sherrod Brown]] are the respective nominees for their parties. The winner will complete the term won in [[2022 United States Senate election in Ohio|2022]] by [[JD Vance]], who resigned in 2025 to become vice president.

Seeking to keep the seat after his appointment, Husted ran unopposed for the Republican nomination. Brown, who represented Ohio in the Senate for three terms until his defeat in [[2024 United States Senate election in Ohio|2024]], won the Democratic nomination against minimal opposition.

This will be the first U.S. Senate special election in Ohio since [[1954 United States Senate special election in Ohio|1954]].

== Background ==
After voting for [[President Barack Obama]] in both [[2008 United States presidential election in Ohio|2008]] and [[2012 United States presidential election in Ohio|2012]], Ohio has trended increasingly Republican in subsequent years and is now considered a moderate to strong [[Red states and blue states|red state]] at the federal and state level. Republicans control all statewide offices, majorities in both chambers of the [[Ohio State Legislature|state legislature]], and hold both [[United States Senate|Senate]] seats. Republicans also have a majority of the state's [[United States House of Representatives|House]] delegation with ten seats compared to five for Democrats.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Grabar|first=Henry|date=November 13, 2018|title=Democrats Proved They Can Win Again in Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania. Why Not Ohio?|url=https://slate.com/business/2018/11/why-ohio-may-not-swing-state.html|access-date=January 18, 2026|website=Slate Magazine|language=en}}</ref>

Republican nominee [[Donald Trump]] won Ohio in [[2016 United States presidential election in Ohio|2016]] and [[2020 United States presidential election in Ohio|2020]] by 8 percentage points, and in [[2024 United States presidential election in Ohio|2024]] grew his margin to 11 percentage points.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schladen |first=Marty |date=2024-11-06 |title=Trump wins Ohio for a third time |url=https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2024/11/05/trump-wins-ohio-for-a-third-time-associated-press-projects/ |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=[[Ohio Capital Journal]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Additionally, Republican [[JD Vance]], now the [[Vice President of the United States|vice president of the United States]], defeated Democrat [[Tim Ryan (Ohio politician)|Tim Ryan]] in the [[2022 United States Senate election in Ohio|2022 U.S. Senate election]] by slightly over 6 points, while Republican [[Bernie Moreno]] defeated then-incumbent Sherrod Brown in the [[2024 United States Senate election in Ohio|2024 U.S. Senate election]] by slightly over 3.5 points.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Evans |first=Nick |date=2024-11-06 |title=Republican Bernie Moreno defeats incumbent Sherrod Brown for Ohio U.S. Senate seat • Ohio Capital Journal |url=https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2024/11/05/republican-bernie-moreno-defeats-incumbent-sherrod-brown-for-ohio-u-s-senate-seat-ap-projects/ |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=[[Ohio Capital Journal]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Interim appointment==
According to Ohio law, if a U.S. Senate seat becomes vacant, the [[List of governors of Ohio|governor]] appoints a replacement who serves until December 15 following the next regularly scheduled statewide election that occurs more than 180 days after the vacancy. A special election to fill the remainder of the term is then held concurrently with that regular state election, which in this case would be the one on [[2026 Ohio elections|November 3, 2026]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Burd |first1=Aaron |title=How J.D. Vance's replacement in U.S. Senate will be picked if he becomes vice president |url=https://www.nbc4i.com/news/your-local-election-hq/how-j-d-vances-replacement-in-u-s-senate-will-be-picked-if-he-becomes-vice-president/ |work=[[WCMH-TV]] |date=July 16, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Filling vacancies in elective offices |url=https://www.ohiosos.gov/globalassets/elections/eoresources/general/fillingvacancies.pdf |publisher=Ohio Secretary of State |access-date=November 6, 2024 |page=2}}</ref> Governor [[Mike DeWine]] chose then-Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted to replace Vance in the Senate.

== General election ==
Data centers have become a major issue in the campaign, and a poll from [[Bowling Green State University]] showed 71% of Ohioans support a temporary ban on new construction of data centers. Brown has criticized Husted for his support of data centers in the past. As lieutenant governor from 2019 to 2025, Husted backed millions of dollars in tax breaks for data center construction projects in Ohio. Husted has defended data centers, saying they bring new jobs and money to rural areas. Husted has described data centers as a "local issue", and Brown has said that the approval of data centers should be decided on the local level.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sivaraman |first=Siddarth |date=August 10, 2026 |title=Ohio U.S. Senate candidates offer contrasting visions for data centers |url=https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2026/08/10/ohio-u-s-senate-candidates-offer-contrasting-visions-for-data-centers/ |access-date=September 29, 2026 |website=Ohio Capital Journal |language=en-US}}</ref>

A September 2026 poll conducted by Bowling Green State University found that 25% of likely Ohio voters incorrectly believed Sherrod Brown was the incumbent U.S. senator from the state, despite him having lost re-election in 2024.<ref>{{cite news|last=Davines|first=Emily|date=September 28, 2026|title=In Ohio, a Humbling Question for Senator Jon Husted: Are You the Incumbent?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/us/politics/john-husted-ohio-president-trump-midterms.html|url-access=subscription|work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>
